newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE fires fresh salvo in European exchange war.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE fires fresh salvo in European exchange war.

text.p: The battle among Europe's bourses for derivatives business after the start of European monetary union in 1999 showed no sign of letup on Wednesday as London's main futures exchange fired a new salvo.
The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) plans to launch medium-term German government bond (Bobl) futures and options contracts in September or October.
"We believe we have already won the battle for short sterm interest rate contracts post 1999," said LIFFE chief executive Daniel Hodson at a news conference.
"We are positioned to win the battle to dominate euro bond contracts, and a major piece in the puzzle is to launch the Bobl," he said.

MATIF last month said it will launch five-year mark bond futures and options, to start trading on May 16, and a spokesman for the French exchange said it had been aware, through its common membership, that a similar LIFFE contract was imminent.
"But we refute the idea that we only launched this contract because LIFFE was planning one," he said.
He said MATIF had introduced its Bobl in order to capitalise on the options skill available on the exchange.

MATIF's president Gerard Pfauwadel has consistently maintained that Paris will have an advantage since unlike London, it is likely to be part of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) from the start. Also stock, debt and currency markets in France will instantly convert to the euro.
A spokeswoman for Germany's Deutsche Terminboerse (DTB) said it was not concerned that the new LIFFE contract would be any threat to the domestic contract.
"We are quite relaxed about this," she said. "We have good liquidity, and an average daily volume of 85,000 contracts."
She also noted that the last time LIFFE ventured into this part of the yield curve, it had been less than successful.
LIFFE's original Bobl contract was launched in early 1993, and was suspended in September 1994.

Hodson said the Bobl market has changed focus significantly since then. He said it used to appear too domestically orientated, with little to offer international investors. But the five-year section of the yield curve has seen rapid growth over the last two years, he said.

Perhaps wary of the earlier failure, LIFFE said it will introduce a new market maker scheme to ensure liquidity. Members can apply through a competitive bidding process to be the designated market market for futures, options or both.
The exchange has the opportunity of terminating that system once daily liquidity reached 25,000 lots per day.

LIFFE was also pinning its hopes that the Bobl options contract would be more liquid than its German rival, since it will be traded through open outcry -- where dealers trade face to face -- rather than through the electronic method favoured in Germany.
"In the end the market will decide," said Hodson.
